ox: Wrong. pH 1 would be 0.1 M HCl. Check the exponent.
Correct. HCl is a strong acid, so it fully dissociates and [H+] = 0.01 = 10^-2 M, giving pH = 2.
Wrong. 12 is the pOH for this solution (14 - 2), not the pH.
Wrong. 0.01 is the concentration, not the pH. pH is the negative log of it.

p: pH = -log[H+], where [H+] is the hydrogen ion concentration in moles per liter. A strong acid breaks apart completely in water.
So [H+] equals the acid concentration. 0.01 M HCl gives [H+] = 10^-2, and pH = 2.

mem: Strong acids: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, HClO4.
Each 10x change in [H+] changes pH by 1.

fm.why: A strong acid fully dissociates, so [H+] equals its concentration.
fm.nc: Write the concentration as a power of 10; the pH is the exponent without the minus sign.

q67.trap: Confusing pH with pOH, or with the concentration value itself.
q67.plain: pH just counts the zeros in the decimal. 0.01 has the 1 in the second place, so pH is 2.

ox: Wrong. This is the pH when the base to acid ratio is 1:10 (more acid than base).
Correct. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log(10) = pKa + 1.
Wrong. pH equals pKa only when [A-] = [HA], a ratio of 1.
Wrong. The relationship is logarithmic, so a ratio of 10 adds 1, not 10.

p: A buffer has a weak acid (HA) and its conjugate base (A-). The equation links pH to the ratio of the two.
When base is 10 times acid, log(10) = 1, so pH is one unit above pKa. pKa is the pH where acid and base are equal.

mem: Ratio 1 gives pH = pKa; ratio 10 gives pKa + 1; ratio 0.1 gives pKa - 1.
More base than acid means pH above pKa.

fm.f: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), where pKa = -log of the acid dissociation constant, [A-] = base concentration, [HA] = acid concentration
fm.why: This is the buffer equation, and the question gives the ratio.
fm.nc: log(10) = 1, so no calculator is needed.

q68.sc: Ratio 10x means plus 1; 100x means plus 2; 1/10 means minus 1.
q68.trap: Reversing the ratio (acid over base) or treating the log as linear.
q68.plain: A seesaw balanced at pKa tilts one notch for each factor of 10 you pile on the base side.

ox: Wrong. Glucose does not dissociate, so i = 1 and the effect is proportional to 0.1.
Wrong. NaCl gives 2 particles (Na+ and Cl-), so i = 2 and the effect is proportional to 0.2.
Correct. CaCl2 gives 3 particles (Ca2+ and two Cl-), so i = 3 and the effect is proportional to 0.3, the largest.
Wrong. MgSO4 gives 2 particles, so 2 x 0.05 = 0.1, which is smaller than 0.3.

p: Dissolved particles lower a solvent's freezing point. This is a colligative property, meaning it depends on the number of particles, not their identity.
Compare i x molality, where i is the number of particles one formula unit makes. The largest product gives the lowest freezing point.

mem: Higher i x m means lower freezing point.

fm.f: dTf = i x Kf x m, where dTf = freezing point drop, i = particles per formula unit, Kf = solvent constant, m = molality (mol/kg)
fm.v: Compare i x m: glucose 1 x 0.1, NaCl 2 x 0.1, CaCl2 3 x 0.1, MgSO4 2 x 0.05
fm.why: Kf is the same for water, so only i x m differs.
fm.nc: Multiply small numbers by hand; Kf cancels in the comparison.

q69.sc: Just compare i x m; skip Kf.
q69.trap: Forgetting to multiply by i, or choosing the highest molality.
q69.plain: The more people crowd onto a dance floor, the harder it is for water molecules to line up and freeze.

ox: Correct. NaCl adds Cl⁻, which AgCl also makes when it dissolves. By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts toward solid AgCl, so less AgCl dissolves.
Wrong. This treats the added salt as helping dissolve things. A shared (common) ion does the opposite and suppresses dissolving.
Wrong. It is true that Ksp stays constant, which is the trap. But Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] stays fixed while [Cl⁻] rises, so [Ag⁺] must fall, and solubility changes.
Wrong. Ksp is an equilibrium constant that changes only with temperature, not with added ions.

p: Solubility is how much solid dissolves. AgCl dissolves a tiny bit: AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻. The Ksp is the product [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] at equilibrium (brackets mean concentration).
If you add a salt with one of the same ions (Cl⁻ from NaCl), the product is pushed too high. The system fixes this by making more solid AgCl, so less dissolves.

mem: Adding a common ion lowers solubility.
q70.sc: See a shared ion added? Pick 'solubility decreases'.
q70.trap: Confusing solubility with Ksp. Ksp stays constant; solubility shifts.
q70.plain: A bus has a fixed number of seats. If lots of people are already standing in the aisle (extra Cl⁻), fewer new people can get on.

ox: Correct. At equivalence all the weak acid has become its conjugate base (A⁻). A⁻ takes H⁺ from water, making OH⁻, so the pH is above 7.
Wrong. pH 7 at equivalence is only for a strong acid with a strong base, where neither product reacts with water.
Wrong. Below 7 happens when a weak base is titrated with a strong acid, because the conjugate acid is left over.
Wrong. pH = pKa is at the half-equivalence point, where half the acid has been converted. Equivalence is later.

p: The equivalence point is when moles of base added equal the moles of acid you started with. For a weak acid HA, all of it is turned into A⁻, its conjugate base (the particle left after losing H⁺).
A⁻ is a weak base. It grabs H⁺ from water, leaving extra OH⁻. More OH⁻ means the pH is above 7.

mem: Weak acid + strong base: equivalence pH > 7.
Weak base + strong acid: equivalence pH < 7.
q71.trap: Assuming equivalence always means pH 7. Look at what is left: the conjugate of the weak partner decides.
q71.plain: After the fight is over, the winner (the stronger side) still leaves a little mess. Here the leftover is a mild base.
